Since rational expressions are quotients in which the variables represent real numbers, the properties of real numbers apply to rational expressions as well, and operations with rational fractions are performed in the same manner as operations with arithmetic fractions. where $$a$$ , $$b$$ , and $$c$$ are any real numbers and $$b$$ and $$c$$ are not zero.

section.heading: Rationalizing Algebraic Fractions
section.paragraph: When the denominator of an algebraic fraction contains sums or differences involving radicals, we may rationalize the denominator—that is, transform the fraction into an equivalent one with a denominator that does not contain radicals. In doing so, we make use of the fact that
$$\begin{array}{l} {{({\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}})({\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b}})} = {{(\sqrt{a})}^{2} - {(\sqrt{b})}^{2}}} \\ {\phantom{({\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}})({\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b}})} = {a - b}} \end{array}$$
This procedure is illustrated in Example 6.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Rationalize the denominator: $$\frac{1}{1 + \sqrt{x}}$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Upon multiplying the numerator and the denominator by $$\left( {1 - \sqrt{x}} \right)$$ , we obtain

$$\begin{matrix} {\frac{1}{1 + \sqrt{x}} = {\frac{1}{1 + \sqrt{x}} \cdot \frac{1 - \sqrt{x}}{1 - \sqrt{x}}} {\frac{1 - \sqrt{x}}{1 - \sqrt{x}} = 1}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{1}{1 + \sqrt{x}}} = \frac{1 - \sqrt{x}}{1 - \left( \sqrt{x} \right)^{2}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{1}{1 + \sqrt{x}}} = \frac{1 - \sqrt{x}}{1 - x}} \end{matrix}$$

section.paragraph: In other situations, it may be necessary to rationalize the numerator of an algebraic expression. In calculus, for example, one encounters the following problem.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Rationalize the numerator: $$\frac{\sqrt{1 + h} - 1}{h}$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: $$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{\sqrt{1 + h} - 1}{h} = {\frac{\sqrt{1 + h} - 1}{h} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{1 + h} + 1}{\sqrt{1 + h} + 1}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{\sqrt{1 + h} - 1}{h}} = \frac{{(\sqrt{1 + h})}^{2} - {(1)}^{2}}{h{({\sqrt{1 + h} + 1})}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{\sqrt{1 + h} - 1}{h}} = \frac{1 + h - 1}{h{({\sqrt{1 + h} + 1})}} \begin{array}{l} {{(\sqrt{1 + h})}^{2} = {\sqrt{1 + h} \cdot \sqrt{1 + h}}} \\ {\phantom{{(\sqrt{1 + h})}^{2}} = {1 + h}} \end{array}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{\sqrt{1 + h} - 1}{h}} = \frac{h}{h{({\sqrt{1 + h} + 1})}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{\sqrt{1 + h} - 1}{h}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + h} + 1}} \end{array}$$

If $$a < b$$ , then $$a + c < b + c$$ .

section.paragraph: Similar properties hold if each inequality sign, $$<$$ , between $$a$$ and $$b$$ and between $$b$$ and $$c$$ is replaced by $$\geq$$ , $$>$$ , or $$\leq$$ . Note that Property 4 says that an inequality sign is reversed if the inequality is multiplied by a negative number.

A real number is a solution of an inequality involving a variable if a true statement is obtained when the variable is replaced by that number. The set of all real numbers satisfying the inequality is called the solution set. We often use interval notation to describe the solution set.

example.heading: Example 9
example.paragraph: Solve the inequality $$x^{2} + 2x - 8 < 0$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Observe that $$x^{2} + 2x - 8 = (x + 4)(x - 2)$$ , so the given inequality is equivalent to the inequality $$(x + 4)(x - 2) < 0$$ . Since the product of two real numbers is negative if and only if the two numbers have opposite signs, we solve the inequality $$(x + 4)(x - 2) < 0$$ by studying the signs of the two factors $$x + 4$$ and $$x - 2$$ . Now, $$x + 4 > 0$$ when $$x > - 4$$ , and $$x + 4 < 0$$ when $$x < - 4$$ . Similarly, $$x - 2 > 0$$ when $$x > 2$$ , and $$x - 2 < 0$$ when $$x < 2$$ . These results are summarized graphically in Figure 2.

image.alt: Details A sign diagram shows a number line labeled x with markings labeled from negative 5 through positive 5. Above the line, there are two rows of plus and minus symbols. In the row for the factor x minus 2, negative signs appear from negative 5 to just before positive 2; 0 is marked above positive 2, and positive signs appear just after 2 up until 5. Similarly, in the row for the factor x + 4, negative signs appear from negative 5 to just before negative 4; 0 is marked above negative 4, and positive signs appear from just after negative 4 to positive 5.

example.paragraph: From Figure 2, we see that the two factors $$x + 4$$ and $$x - 2$$ have opposite signs when and only when $$x$$ lies strictly between $$- 4$$ and $$2$$ . Therefore, the required solution is the interval $$( - 4,2)$$ .

example.heading: Example 10
example.paragraph: Solve the inequality $$\frac{x + 1}{x - 1} \geq 0$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The quotient $$(x + 1) \slash (x - 1)$$ is strictly positive if and only if both the numerator and the denominator have the same sign. The signs of $$x + 1$$ and $$x - 1$$ are shown in Figure 3.

image.alt: Details A sign diagram shows a number line labeled x with markings labeled negative 4 through positive 4. Above the line, there are two rows of plus and minus symbols. In the row for the factor x minus 1, negative signs appear from negative 4 to just before positive 1; 0 is marked above positive 1, and positive signs appear just after 1 up until 4. Similarly, in the row for the factor x + 1, negative signs appear from negative 4 to just before negative 1; 0 is marked above negative 1, and positive signs appear from just after negative 1 to positive 4.

example.paragraph: From Figure 3, we see that $$x + 1$$ and $$x - 1$$ have the same sign if $$x < - 1$$ or $$x > 1$$ . The quotient $$(x + 1) \slash (x - 1)$$ is equal to zero if $$x = - 1$$ . Therefore, the required solution is the set of all $$x$$ in the intervals $$( - \infty, - 1\rbrack$$ and $$(1,\infty)$$ .

section.paragraph: Since $$- a$$ is a positive number when $$a$$ is negative, it follows that the absolute value of a number is always nonnegative. For example, $$\left| 5 \middle| = 5 \right.$$ and $$\left| - 5 \middle| = - ( - 5) = 5 \right.$$ . Geometrically, $$|a|$$ is the distance between the origin and the point on the number line that represents the number $$a$$ (Figure 4).

example.heading: Example 13
example.paragraph: Solve the inequalities $$\left| x \middle| \leq 5 \right.$$ and $$\left| x \middle| \geq 5 \right.$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: First, we consider the inequality $$\left| x \middle| \leq 5 \right.$$ . If $$x \geq 0$$ , then $$\left| x \middle| = x \right.$$ , so $$\left| x \middle| \leq 5 \right.$$ implies $$x \leq 5$$ in this case. On the other hand, if $$x < 0$$ , then $$\left| x \middle| = - x \right.$$ , so $$\left| x \middle| \leq 5 \right.$$ implies $$- x \leq 5$$ or $$x \geq - 5$$ . Thus, $$\left| x \middle| \leq 5 \right.$$ means $$- 5 \leq x \leq 5$$ (Figure 5a). To obtain an alternative solution, observe that $$|x|$$ is the distance from the point $$x$$ to zero, so the inequality $$\left| x \middle| \leq 5 \right.$$ implies immediately that $$- 5 \leq x \leq 5$$ .

The line to the left of negative 5 is shaded and the line to the right of positive 5 is shaded, in both cases including the endpoints negative 5 and positive 5.

example.paragraph: Next, the inequality $$\left| x \middle| \geq 5 \right.$$ states that the distance from $$x$$ to zero is greater than or equal to $$5$$ . This observation yields the result $$x \geq 5$$ or $$x \leq - 5$$ (Figure 5b).

example.heading: Example 14
example.paragraph: Solve the inequality $$\left| 2x - 3 \middle| \leq 1 \right.$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The inequality $$\left| 2x - 3 \middle| \leq 1 \right.$$ is equivalent to the inequalities $$- 1 \leq 2x - 3 \leq 1$$ (see Example 13). Thus, $$2 \leq 2x \leq 4$$ and $$1 \leq x \leq 2$$ . The solution is therefore given by the set of all $$x$$ in the interval $$\lbrack 1,2\rbrack$$ (Figure 6).
